strengths: Creative and novel exploration of repurposing a meta-trained tabular transformer (TabPFN) as a zero-shot, gradient-free Q-function approximator within the Fitted Q Iteration (FQI) framework.

Insightful theoretical discussion analyzing how TabPFN-RL violates the core assumptions of the TabPFN prior (i.i.d. transitions, bootstrapped Bellman targets, and policy-induced distribution shift) while still exhibiting generalization capability.

Addresses the critical context-length limitations of in-context learning in RL by proposing and evaluating several context-truncation heuristics (such as Naive De-duplication) to enable continual learning.
weaknesses: Highly limited evaluation restricted to three very basic, low-dimensional classic control tasks (CartPole, MountainCar, and Acrobot) which do not represent the complexity of modern RL benchmarks.

Heavy reliance on custom, dense reward shaping to achieve reasonable performance, which contradicts the paper's introduction stating that gradient-free methods are particularly promising for sparse-reward environments.

Lack of standard Fitted Q Iteration (FQI) baselines. Since TabPFN-RL is essentially FQI using TabPFN as the regressor, it is crucial to compare it against FQI using other standard tabular regression models (such as Random Forests, Extra Trees, or XGBoost) to isolate the benefits of TabPFN.

The DQN baseline appears to perform poorly (e.g., failing to reach the maximum score of 500 on CartPole-v1, which standard DQN typically solves very quickly), suggesting the baseline might be undertuned or negatively affected by the custom reward shaping.

The quadratic self-attention bottleneck ($O(B^2)$) of TabPFN at a context budget of up to $B=8096$ incurs massive computational and latency overhead during online interaction, making the method far less computationally efficient in practice than standard parametric RL methods.

strengths: Explores a highly creative and novel concept: repurposing TabPFN (a prior-fitted network for tabular data) as a gradient-free Q-function approximator in reinforcement learning.

Identifies and addresses a critical roadblock in in-context reinforcement learning—namely, the fixed context budget—and designs/evaluates multiple heuristic truncation operators (Latest, ND, ED, RV) to support continual learning.

Features a thoughtful theoretical discussion detailing the mismatch between RL data characteristics (bootstrapped labels, non-i.i.d. transitions, distribution shift) and the i.i.d. assumptions baked into TabPFN's prior.
weaknesses: Extremely limited empirical evaluation: The method is only tested on three very simple classic control environments (CartPole, MountainCar, and Acrobot) which are low-dimensional and easily solved by basic methods.

Heavy reliance on customized reward shaping: The authors acknowledge that the model performs poorly with sparse rewards, necessitating custom dense reward shaping functions for all environments. This severely limits the generalization and practicality of the proposed method.

Lack of computational cost and wall-clock time analysis: Despite claiming the method is 'fast and computationally efficient' in the abstract, transformer inference scales quadratically with the context size. For the recommended context budget of B=8096, running a forward pass at every single action step is likely extremely slow and computationally demanding compared to tiny gradient-based MLPs, but no wall-clock times are provided to support the efficiency claims.

The comparison with DQN is somewhat overstated, as DQN can easily solve these simple environments with minimal tuning and standard rewards, whereas TabPFN-RL requires highly specific hyperparameters (e.g., context budgets, epsilon decay, percentiles) and engineered rewards to succeed.

strengths: Highly creative core concept of using a pre-trained tabular foundation model (TabPFN) as a gradient-free Q-function approximator via in-context Fitted Q Iteration (FQI).

Insightful theoretical discussion regarding the 'Task-Prior Mismatch', explaining why TabPFN generalizes to sequential, non-i.i.d., and bootstrapped RL data despite being trained on i.i.d. tabular data.
Proposes and analyzes various context truncation heuristics (such as Naive De-duplication) to mitigate the physical context size limitation of transformer-based in-context RL.
weaknesses: The empirical evaluation is restricted to three simple, low-dimensional classic control tasks (CartPole, MountainCar, Acrobot), which does not sufficiently demonstrate the scalability of the method.

The proposed method heavily relies on hand-designed dense reward shaping (as described in the Appendix) because it struggles with sparse rewards. This limits its applicability to more general RL problems where reward shaping is difficult or unknown.

The computational complexity of the proposed algorithm is extremely high and not analyzed. Running 60 iterations of FQI on a context of up to 8096 transitions requires 60 * 8096 * |A| forward passes of a transformer with a context length of up to 8096. The paper lacks wall-clock time comparisons with DQN, which are crucial given the quadratic complexity of transformer self-attention.
The implementation details in the main text could be clearer regarding how the FQI target bootstrapping is performed step-by-step using TabPFN without causing massive memory overhead or slow-downs.

strengths: An elegant and creative conceptual framework (ICR-RL) that reduces reinforcement learning to in-context regression, utilizing general-purpose pre-trained tabular models (like TabPFN) without requiring any gradient-based fine-tuning or RL-specific trajectory pre-training.

A thorough exploration of context engineering and compression techniques (e.g., Naive De-duplication) that successfully addresses the context-window bottleneck of Transformer-based models in sequential decision tasks.
Demonstrates the framework's flexibility by showing it can be integrated with different in-context regression backbones, such as TabICL and TabFlex.
weaknesses: Extremely limited empirical evaluation, restricted only to three simple, low-dimensional classic control toy environments (CartPole, MountainCar, Acrobot).

Strong reliance on dense, hand-crafted reward shaping. The authors note that the method struggles significantly with standard sparse rewards, suggesting a high level of brittleness to the reward signal.

The manuscript claims support for continuous action spaces (e.g., Section 3 and Table 1), but this is neither formulated nor evaluated. Performing the Bellman maximization step over continuous actions using a black-box tabular regressor like TabPFN is non-trivial, and its feasibility remains unproven in this work.

The baseline algorithms (such as PPO and TRPO) seem severely undertuned. For example, standard PPO should easily solve CartPole-v1 (reaching the maximum reward of 500), but in Figure 2, it struggles to exceed a reward of 100.

Lacks wall-clock runtime or computational overhead analyses. Running iterative in-context Fitted Q-Iteration (ICR-FQI) with a quadratic-complexity Transformer model in the inner loop likely introduces substantial latency compared to standard deep RL methods.

strengths: Novel concept: The idea of reducing online reinforcement learning to in-context regression using a general-purpose tabular foundation model (like TabPFN) without any RL-specific pre-training or gradient updates is creative and interesting.
Context management exploration: The paper systematically addresses the issue of context budget constraints in transformers by exploring and evaluating different pruning and deduplication strategies.

Detailed analysis of prior mismatch: Section 5 provides a thoughtful discussion on the theoretical mismatch between the i.i.d. assumption under which TabPFN was trained and the non-stationary, correlated nature of RL trajectories.
weaknesses: Heavily reliant on custom reward shaping: The authors state that ICR-RL fails under sparse rewards, necessitating custom dense reward-shaping functions for all three environments (Appendix B.2). This significantly reduces the autonomy of the agent, as designing these rewards requires substantial domain expertise.

Weak baseline performance and potential misconfiguration: The performance of standard baselines like PPO and TRPO in Figure 2 and Figure 10 is surprisingly poor. For example, on CartPole-v1, PPO and TRPO fail to reach the maximum reward, and on Acrobot-v1, they underperform significantly. Standard implementations (e.g., Stable-Baselines3 with default parameters) typically solve these environments quickly and reliably. This suggests either a sub-optimal baseline configuration or that the custom reward shaping negatively impacted the standard algorithms.

Limited evaluation scope: The empirical evaluation is restricted to three very simple, low-dimensional classic control tasks (CartPole, MountainCar, Acrobot). To prove the viability of a 'foundation model for RL' approach, evaluation on more complex benchmarks (such as Atari or continuous robotic control) is necessary.

High inference-time computational overhead: Running a full Transformer forward pass (with quadratic complexity relative to the context size) at every single environment step to compute Q-values is highly inefficient compared to standard deep RL networks. The manuscript lacks a thorough wall-clock time comparison with baseline methods.

Unaddressed hyperparameter complexity: While the paper claims to avoid the hyperparameter sensitivity of gradient-based deep RL, the proposed method introduces many of its own sensitive hyperparameters, including the context budget B, epsilon-decay schedules, quantile filtering thresholds, reward perturbation noise scale, and FQI iteration parameters.

strengths: An elegant and novel conceptual reduction: representing Fitted Q-Iteration (FQI) as In-Context Regression (ICR) using general-purpose tabular foundation models (like TabPFN/TabICL) without any gradient updates or task-specific fine-tuning.
Proposes and systematically evaluates several context-engineering techniques (e.g., Naive De-duplication) to effectively manage the quadratic complexity of transformers under limited context budgets.
The paper is generally well-written, with clear explanations of the algorithms (ICR-FQI and ICR-RL) and comprehensive appendix sections containing hyperparameters and implementation details.
weaknesses: The evaluation is restricted to three very simple, low-dimensional classic control environments (CartPole, MountainCar, Acrobot), which limits the demonstrated scalability of the approach.

There is a heavy reliance on handcrafted dense reward shaping. The authors admit that the method struggles with sparse rewards, and the necessity of customized reward functions makes it difficult to assess general applicability.

The baseline performances for PPO and TRPO in Figure 2 appear anomalously low (e.g., PPO failing to solve CartPole-v1, which is typically solved very quickly by default PPO). This raises questions about the tuning and fairness of the baseline comparisons.

Lack of absolute wall-clock time comparisons. Running a deep transformer forward pass with large context sizes (e.g., 512 to 8096) at every decision step is likely orders of magnitude slower than running standard MLP-based RL agents, which is a major practical bottleneck not fully quantified in the main text.
